lead: Feature selection keeps a smaller set of the original columns before a model is trained. It exists because extra features add noise, cost and overfitting risk. Correlation analysis checks how features move with the target and with each other, so redundant or weak columns can be spotted. It is used in credit scoring, churn prediction, medical tests and sensor data. The tools are filter, wrapper and embedded selection, with Pearson correlation as the main filter.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.5 for dimensionality reduction, and Unit 2, Regularization: ridge and lasso, for the L1 penalty.

blocks.text: Feature selection chooses a subset of the original features and drops the rest. A feature is a column such as age, income or a sensor reading. The target is the value to predict, for example loan default. The output is a smaller table with the same rows and fewer columns. No new column is created. This separates it from PCA, which builds new axes.

Why? More features increase training time and memory. Some are noisy or duplicated. A model can fit noise in training data and fail on new data. Selection also makes a model easier to explain; a bank can say which few applicant details drove a decision.

Merits: faster models, less overfitting, clearer reports. Demerits: information in dropped features is lost, selection can be unstable on small data, and a wrong filter can remove a feature that only helps in combination.
A common warning is data leakage. Choose features using training data only, then apply the same list to test data. Some syllabi call this feature subset selection.

Correlation analysis measures how two numeric variables move together. For features, compute it in two directions: each feature with the target y, and each feature with every other feature. A high absolute value with y marks a useful linear feature. A high absolute value between two features marks redundancy.

blocks.where: r is the Pearson correlation; cov(X,Y) is the covariance of X and Y; σ<sub>X</sub> and σ<sub>Y</sub> are their standard deviations. r lies from −1 to 1.

blocks.text: r = 1 means a perfect positive straight-line relation; r = −1 means a perfect negative one; r = 0 means no linear association. A filter computes r(X<sub>j</sub>, y) and keeps features with |r| ≥ threshold. 0.5 is common but data-dependent. Variance threshold drops near-constant columns. Chi-square tests a categorical feature against a class. Mutual information captures nonlinear dependence.
The figure is a correlation matrix. X1 has r = 0.82 with y, X2 has 0.05, X3 has −0.78, and X1 and X3 have −0.91. X1 and X3 pass a 0.5 filter; X2 does not. X1 and X3 are also redundant as a pair.
Pearson r measures linear association only. A feature can have r ≈ 0 with y and still help through a curve or an interaction. Also, r is not causation.

Filter methods are fast and model-free. Wrapper methods use a model's accuracy to score subsets. Forward selection starts with no features and adds the best one each round. Backward elimination starts with all features and removes the worst. RFE, recursive feature elimination, fits a model, removes the weakest features, and repeats.
Wrappers catch interactions but are expensive: each round retrains the model. Use cross-validation inside the loop, or small data can make the choice unstable.

Embedded methods select during training. L1 lasso adds λΣ|w<sub>j</sub>| to the loss; it pushes some weights exactly to zero, so those features leave a linear model. See Unit 2, Regularization: ridge and lasso. Tree importance from a random forest ranks features by impurity reduction; permutation importance measures the drop when a feature is shuffled.

Choose by budget. A filter is good for many columns and a quick first pass. A wrapper is good when accuracy matters and training is cheap. L1 is good for a linear model with many features. Always fit selection on training data and apply the same list to test data.

spec.title: Correlation matrix
spec.aria: A correlation table for features X1, X2, X3 and target y shows X1 and X3 strongly linked to y and to each other, while X2 is near zero.

examples.question: A dataset has three features X1, X2, X3 and target y. The correlations with y are r(X1,y)=0.82, r(X2,y)=0.05 and r(X3,y)=−0.78. Also r(X1,X3)=−0.91. A filter keeps a feature when |r(feature,y)| ≥ 0.5. List the selected features, and flag any redundancy using |r| ≥ 0.5 between features.
steps: Compare with 0.5: X1 has 0.82 ≥ 0.5, so keep X1. X2 has 0.05 < 0.5, so drop X2. X3 has 0.78 ≥ 0.5, so keep X3. Selected count = 2.
Check redundancy: |r(X1,X3)| = |−0.91| = 0.91. Since 0.91 ≥ 0.5, X1 and X3 are redundant as a pair; their link is a strong negative linear one.
Practical action: keep one of X1 and X3, or combine them with PCA. Note the negative sign: higher X3 goes with lower y on average.
examples.answer: The filter selects X1 and X3 (2 features); X1 and X3 are redundant because |r| = 0.91 ≥ 0.5.
examples.check:
r1y = 0.82
r2y = 0.05
r3y = -0.78
r13 = -0.91
th = 0.5
sel = []
for name, r in [('X1', r1y), ('X2', r2y), ('X3', r3y)]:
    a = abs(r)
    print(round(a, 2))
    if a >= th:
        sel.append(name)
print(len(sel))
print(round(abs(r13), 2))

traps: A correlation of 0 does not mean no relation; it means no linear relation. A curved relation can have r ≈ 0.
Use |r| when comparing a negative correlation with a positive one. −0.8 is stronger than 0.3.
r(X,Y) is not causation and not a model score. A feature can correlate with y through another feature.
Two features can be redundant for a linear model but still useful in a tree or interaction model; do not delete blindly.
Compute correlations and selection on training data only. Using the full data leaks test information.

quiz.q: Define feature selection. How does it differ from PCA?
quiz.a: Feature selection keeps a subset of the original columns. PCA makes new axes; feature selection creates no new feature.

quiz.q: Why can a feature with |r| with y below 0.5 still help a model?
quiz.a: r detects only linear association. The feature may act through a curve or an interaction with another feature, which a nonlinear model can use.

quiz.q: For target y, r(A,y)=0.70, r(B,y)=−0.40, r(C,y)=0.10. A |r|≥0.5 filter selects which features?
quiz.a: |0.70| = 0.70, keep A. |−0.40| = 0.40, drop B. |0.10| = 0.10, drop C. Selected: A only.

quiz.q: Two features F1 and F2 have r(F1,F2)=0.95 and both have |r|≥0.5 with y. What is the issue and one fix?
quiz.a: They carry almost the same linear information, so the model gets redundant columns and unstable weights. Keep one, or use PCA or L1.

quiz.q: Given cov(X,Y)=8, σ<sub>X</sub>=4 and σ<sub>Y</sub>=2, find the Pearson correlation r.
Compare filter and wrapper feature selection.
quiz.a: A filter ranks features before training using a statistic such as |r|; it is fast and model-free. A wrapper trains a model on candidate subsets, such as forward selection; it is slower but catches interactions.

quiz.q: Why does L1 lasso remove some features?
quiz.a: The penalty λΣ|w<sub>j</sub>| makes small weights shrink to exactly zero, so those features get zero coefficient and are dropped from a linear model.

quiz.q: Name two embedded feature selection methods.
quiz.a: L1 lasso and tree importance, for example random forest impurity importance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern pipelines use mutual information or model-based importance such as Boruta and SHAP to rank features beyond linear r. Stability selection repeats selection on resamples to avoid lucky one-off choices. Search for scikit-learn SelectKBest, RFECV, LassoCV and permutation importance for runnable examples.
